title: Fifty-one years of a two-letter trademark, 29 moments
lede: From an old registration to a canceled one, with about sixteen months of soda in between. Filter by thread.

events.title: OK is first used on soft drinks
events.text: The date of first use in commerce given in a US trademark registration for OK for soft drinks, listed under Coca-Cola’s name. We do not know what product it was used on.

events.title: The first OK registration
events.text: Registration No. 1,093,933 is issued. Coca-Cola’s 1994 application claims ownership of it.

events.title: Sergio Zyman leaves
events.text: He had been senior vice president of marketing for Coca-Cola USA. The Believer later calls New Coke his “last brainstorm.”

events.title: Zyman returns as chief marketing officer
events.text: After seven years as a consultant, according to Coca-Cola’s annual report on Form 10-K.

events.title: A year of field study
events.text: Coca-Cola says the campaign was tuned during a year of research among teenagers, on top of a two-year “Global Teenager” program with MIT graduate students.

events.title: “Obey Your Thirst”
events.text: Coca-Cola launches a Sprite campaign that, in Time’s words, “pointedly refuses to overpromise.” Fruitopia is introduced the same year.

events.title: First new trademark application
events.text: Coca-Cola files to register OK for soft drinks, syrups and concentrates. It abandons this application, and a second one filed June 27, on February 3, 1995.

events.title: Introduced in New York
events.text: Zyman presents “a cola-colored, full-calorie soda” for 12- to 25-year-olds. Reporters taste “a slight orange or citrus flavor.”

events.title: “Admittedly not fully formed”
events.text: Advertising Age reports the brand will reach the market within 30 days.

events.title: First sale
events.text: The date of first use in commerce in the trademark record. The Washington Post later says the drink had been test-marketed “since May.”

events.title: Chain letters in the mail
events.text: Coca-Cola mails letters in its target markets telling recipients to show them “to six close friends.” Dated from Time’s “two weeks ago.”

events.title: A cool focus group
events.text: In Minneapolis, 15-to-17-year-olds eventually warm to the taste. The 18-to-20-year-olds never do. Both groups keep calling the 800 number.

events.title: NPR: “Who cares?”
events.text: On All Things Considered, consultant Tom Pirko says taste falls “way down in the hierarchy” of why people choose a soft drink. The drink is on sale in Austin, Denver, Minneapolis–St. Paul, Seattle “and a few other cities.”

events.title: Time: “Will Teens Buy It?”
events.text: Nine test cities, four can designs chosen from more than 50, print and TV ads starting that week, and a plan to go national in the summer and abroad by year-end.

events.title: The application that sticks
events.text: Coca-Cola files for the red-boxed OK mark, claiming first use on May 6.

events.title: “Dismal sales” in Minneapolis
events.text: The Washington Post finds a store that has not sold one 12-pack and another where the distributor has pulled the product. Coca-Cola says the hotline has taken more than a million calls and announces plans for four other countries.

events.title: The hotline’s scheduled return
events.text: Callers in early September are told the interactive services are paused until this date “for purely arbitrary reasons.” We could not confirm what happened on it.

events.title: One mention in the 10-K
events.text: Coca-Cola’s annual report for 1994 lists “OK soda” among its soft drink products. Advertising for the whole company was $1,308 million.

events.title: Trademark published for opposition
events.text: A routine step in the registration, one week before the end.

events.title: “We decided not to continue it”
events.text: Spokesman Randy Donaldson says Coca-Cola has sold more than one million cases and will phase the drink out of its test markets. The Times dates his remarks to “Monday.”

events.title: “Phasing Out a Soda”
events.text: The New York Times prints the news in four sentences.

events.title: Gone from the list
events.text: The 10-K for 1995 names Coca-Cola’s soft drinks without OK. Barq’s, bought that year, is new.

events.title: Registered, eighteen months late
events.text: The Patent and Trademark Office registers the OK mark to Coca-Cola after a concurrent-use proceeding.

events.title: “The nine-city campaign fizzled”
events.text: Time cites OK in a feature on how marketers misjudged Generation X.

events.title: The 1978 registration expires
events.text: It was not renewed.

events.title: The 1997 registration is canceled
events.text: Coca-Cola filed no declaration of continued use. Fruitopia is phased out in the United States the same year.

events.title: “The cans are quite valuable”
events.text: Daniel Clowes tells Mother Jones the eyes on his can were Charles Manson’s. Time puts OK in its “Top 10 Bad Beverage Ideas.”

events.title: The Believer’s long look back
events.text: Michael Schulman interviews the campaign’s creators twenty years on.

events.title: Still gone
events.text: Both registrations show as dead in the USPTO’s database when checked on October 8, 2026. We found no re-release.
